text: Ridgeline Outfitters' four-lesson capstone pulled on every chapter of this course, not just the two it most obviously resembles on the surface. This lesson traces each decision from the capstone back to the specific earlier chapter that actually made it possible, then closes the course and points to what's next in the Cloud Engineer to Cloud Architect path.

Chapter 1 is why metrics, logs, and traces needed no introduction when Lesson 29 instrumented order-service. Chapter 2's Azure Monitor deep dive is why configure_azure_monitor and a KQL query across AppTraces, AppMetrics, and AppDependencies felt like reaching for a known tool. Chapter 3's CloudWatch and X-Ray skills are the same pattern on the other major cloud, the reason this course isn't locked to one vendor.

Chapter 4 is why Lesson 30 pinned the cost view onto the same dashboard as its Grafana panels, instead of an isolated chart -- a dashboard should answer a real question. Chapter 5 is the entire backbone of that lesson: the tagging taxonomy and the staged budget plus anomaly pattern, the FinOps framework's Inform stage done for real.

Chapter 6's right-sizing discipline is why the node pool in Lesson 31 was ever a candidate for downsizing -- a correct cost signal on its own. What it doesn't teach alone, and what Lesson 31 adds, is that a correct signal still needs a reliability reviewer before it becomes a merged change.

Chapter 7 is why Lesson 31's incident was legible at all. SLIs, SLOs, and error budgets turned four minutes of latency into 19 of 43 error-budget minutes consumed, and the blameless postmortem process shaped a root-cause analysis that fixed a review gate instead of assigning blame.

Across four lessons, Ridgeline instrumented a real application, built a real cost dashboard next to its reliability panels, and worked through an incident where a correct, well-reasoned cost decision still broke an SLO because nobody connected the two. That's the real point of this entire course: observability, dashboards, and FinOps are one operating practice, not three. This course is now complete; the Advanced Specialization stage continues from here.
